fetched_contents.text: Pulmonary embolism masked by symptoms of mental disorders Abstract Purpose The objective of this article is to draw attention to an unusual clinical manifestation of pulmonary embolism (PE) as symptoms suggesting an underlying mental disorder. This seems all the more important since PE is one of the most common causes of potentially preventable hospital deaths and delayed diagnosis of PE in patients consulted at emergency departments has been shown to be most common in elderly patients and the ones presenting with significantly altered mental status. Views PE is a life-threatening condition that requires prompt diagnosis and appropriate management. There is no symptom that can be found characteristic for PE. Clinical picture of this condition is varied and may resemble many other disorders. The article emphasises that PE may also manifest with psychopathological symptoms that mimic psychiatric emergencies. Three most common groups of psychopathological symptoms that can mask a developing PE, such as panic attacks, symptoms of psychosis, and catatonia, are discussed here based on the literature review. Conclusions Particular care must be exercised while evaluating such a patient because initial misdiagnosis results in the patient being referred to a mental health care unit instead of a unit treating somatic disorders. There are no diagnostic or treatment facilities in large psychiatric hospitals to assist such a patient. This, in turn, leads to a significant delay in management and, consequently, to major complications or death. Keywords: psychosis, pulmonary embolism, catatonia, emergency, panic attacks INTRODUCTION Pulmonary embolism (PE) is one of the components of venous thromboembolism (VTE). It is a blockage or obstruction of a pulmonary artery or sections of its branches by an embolic material, being a thrombus, originating in majority of cases from deep veins of lower limbs. Acute PE is the most common life-threatening cardiovascular disorder which is associated with mortality of 30% when managed incorrectly [1]. PE is one of the most common causes of potentially preventable hospital deaths [2]. There are no symptoms specific to PE. The clinical picture is varied and may resemble many other disorders. Patients most often complain of dyspnoea. It may be sudden and severe or mild and transient in case of central and peripheral PE, respectively. Whenever dyspnoea is exacerbated in patients with chronic lung diseases or circulatory failure, PE should be taken into account as one of the causes. Embolism must also be considered in case of chest pain, being another common symptom. It usually results from irritation of the pleura by peripheral emboli, making the chest pain pleuritic. Patients describe it as sharp, stabbing, usually located on the sides of the chest, often unilaterally. It may exacerbate during inspiration, cough, or trunk movements. The pain may radiate to the intercostal region. Less often, in case of central PE, pain may be stenocardial. It is then described as a crushing, burning, or squeezing sensation, located retrosternally. It may worsen on exertion and radiate to the neck, jaw, shoulder, elbow, or epigastrium. Other possible symptoms may include but not be limited to cough (usually dry), syncope or presyncope and/or haemoptysis. Physical examination reveals tachypnoea and tachycardia in more than half of patients. Arterial blood oxygen saturation (SaO2) is reduced in ≥ 60% of patients. One third of PE cases present with symptoms of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in lower limbs, such as swelling of the lower leg, pain on pressure in the calf, increased warmth in the limb, dilatation of superficial veins which persists when the limb is elevated, and low-grade fever/fever. Given the above description, there is no symptom that may be found characteristic for PE. The following disorders are listed most often in the context of differential diagnosis with PE: acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, cardiac tamponade, ventricular septal rupture, cardiogenic shock, pneumonia and pleurisy, asthma, pneumothorax, and intercostal nerve neuralgia [1]. It is pointed out that PE may manifest also as psychopathological symptoms that mimic psychiatric emergencies. This often results in misdiagnosis and patients being referred to mental health units instead of units treating somatic disorders. This, in turn, leads to a significant delay in diagnosis and treatment, and – consequently – often to the patient’s death. Delayed diagnosis of PE in patients consulted at emergency departments has been shown to be most common in older patients and the ones presenting with significantly altered mental status [3]. PSYCHOPATHOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS MASKING PULMONARY EMBOLISM Panic attacks Repeated panic attacks are regularly observed in patients with anxiety disorder presenting with anxiety attacks; they can be reported in patients with other mental disorders or be caused by a substance (such as a drug) or a general medical condition. A panic attack is an episode of intense fear with various somatic symptoms, with the most frequent being shortness of breath, tachycardia, and chest pain. These symptoms may also suggest PE, which can coexist with panic attacks. Statistical data on the prevalence of PE in patients who reported to a doctor because of panic attacks are not available. However, PE has been shown to be less frequently suspected, both in psychiatric emergency rooms and emergency departments, when anxiety disorder seems to be the most likely alternative diagnosis [4]. Some patients report panic attacks with prevailing respiratory symptoms. The threshold of response to stimuli that can induce a panic attack, such as hyperventilation, inhalation of 35% carbon dioxide, holding one’s breath, sodium lactate, and caffeine, is in these patients lower as compared to patients with panic attacks without respiratory symptoms [5, 6]. For more information, see the section on Management while awaiting admission. * A recent history of ACS, who have developed further chest pain. * Consider admitting people with suspected ACS if pain has resolved and there are signs of complications. Use clinical judgement to decide whether emergency or urgent referral is appropriate. * For information on admission criteria for other conditions, see the CKS topics on Pulmonary embolus, Asthma, Chest infections - adult, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Breathlessness, Palpitations, Heart failure - chronic, Acute pancreatitis, and Acute cholecystitis. They have the name "vital" as their measurement and assessment is the critical first step for any clinical evaluation. The first set of clinical examinations is an evaluation of the vital signs of the patient. Triage of patients in an urgent/prompt care or an emergency department is based on their vital signs as it tells the physician the degree of derangement that is happening from the baseline. Healthcare providers must understand the various physiologic and pathologic processes affecting these sets of measurements and their proper interpretation. If we use a triage method where we select patients without determining their vital signs, it may not give us a reflection of the urgency of the patient's presentation.[1] The degree of vital sign abnormalities may also predict the long-term patient health outcomes, return emergency department visits, and frequency of readmission to hospitals, and utilization of healthcare resources. When to treat as an emergency versus when to observe

In this situation, the nurse should treat chest tightness as an emergency if there is a clear sign of acute decompensation or a high-risk condition, and observe more cautiously if the patient appears stable with no immediate red flags. The evidence supports using vital signs and clinical judgment together rather than relying on chest tightness alone.

### Specific vital-sign thresholds or findings that justify immediate intervention
The clearest thresholds are the ones in the CKS chest-pain management guidance: respiratory rate over 30 breaths per minute, tachycardia over 130 beats per minute, systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg or diastolic less than 60 mmHg, oxygen saturation less than 92%, central cyanosis, altered level of consciousness, and raised temperature above 38.5°C. These are the specific vital-sign findings that justify immediate assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation and urgent admission [N2-F2]. The NICE guideline also notes that suspected ACS, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, aortic dissection, and ruptured oesophagus require immediate admission because of high risk of death or serious morbidity [N2-F2]. In other words, if any of those findings are present, the patient should be treated as an emergency.

### Nursing triage criteria for chest tightness without clear emergency signs
When chest tightness is present but there are no clear emergency signs, the nurse should still treat the patient as potentially unstable and follow triage-based principles. The StatPearls evidence says triage in urgent or emergency settings is based on vital signs and that determining vital signs is the critical first step for any clinical evaluation [N4-F4]. The Acute Chest Pain Care Guide adds that stable vital signs, a physical exam that is unremarkable, and symptoms free during evaluation and monitoring are consistent with non-cardiac chest pain, and the patient can be evaluated and managed accordingly [N4-R4]. So the nurse should not wait for all symptoms to resolve or assume stability based on chest tightness alone; rather, the patient should be triaged based on baseline vital signs and clinical condition.

### What to observe, how often, and what to document
Observation should be guided by the triage framework. The CKS guidance emphasizes physiological assessment: blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature, breathing rate, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness [N2-F2]. It also recommends that these assessments are repeated as needed and that early warning scores are used to determine timing of next observations [N4-F4]. In practice, the nurse should document baseline vital signs, respiratory effort, level of distress, and any changes in symptoms. If the patient is in the psychiatric ward, documentation should also include any psychosocial factors that might affect interpretation, such as the patient’s mental state, history of anxiety or panic, and any family history relevant to chest discomfort. The nurse should observe frequently enough to detect deterioration, especially because early warning scores and frequent reassessment are associated with faster detection of clinical deterioration [N4-F4].

### Bottom line for a senior nurse
In short: treat as an emergency if there are any of the high-risk vital-sign findings or clinical features listed above; otherwise, observe closely, repeat vital signs, and reassess frequently while keeping the patient under close supervision. The patient should not be assumed stable simply because chest tightness is the main complaint [N4-F4][N2-F2].

What chest tightness might mean clinically in this patient

In this 41-year-old psychiatric inpatient, chest tightness is most likely explained by a combination of non-cardiac and psychosomatic factors, but the psychiatric context also raises the need for careful red-flag screening.

### Most likely non-cardiac explanations such as anxiety, panic attack, or hyperventilation
The most likely non-cardiac explanation is anxiety or a panic attack. The PMC article on panic attacks notes that panic attacks are episodes of intense fear with frequent somatic symptoms, including shortness of breath, tachycardia, and chest pain [N1-F1]. Another source specifically states that asthma and panic have similar symptoms, including chest tightness, shortness of breath, and feelings of intense fear [N3-F3]. The same source also says asthma and panic attacks may both cause difficulty breathing and chest tightness, but they have different triggers and effects [N3-R5]. Because the patient is a psychiatric inpatient, hyperventilation and panic attacks are especially plausible, as psychiatric patients can present with chest tightness that mimics organic disease [N1-F1][N3-R3].

### Red flags that suggest serious cardiac or pulmonary disease
The evidence clearly identifies red flags that could point to serious disease. The pulmonary-embolism article says chest pain is a common symptom of PE, and that PE may present with pleuritic chest pain, pain exacerbated by inspiration, cough, or trunk movements, or, less commonly, with crushing, burning, or squeezing retrosternal pain [N1-F1]. The heart-attack warning signs include chest discomfort, arm, neck, and jaw pain, shortness of breath, and more [N1-R5]. The CKS guidance also emphasizes that unstable vital signs and serious clinical features suggest a serious cause of chest pain [N2-F2]. For this patient, the red flags include any of the following: sudden worsening, associated shortness of breath, chest pain that is pleuritic or crushing, new symptoms such as sweating, dizziness, or pain radiating to the arm, or any of the high-risk vital-sign thresholds discussed earlier [N1-F1][N1-R5][N2-F2].

### How psychiatric context may influence the presentation and interpretation
The psychiatric context is important because it can both mimic and obscure organic disease. The PMC article explicitly states that PE may manifest with psychopathological symptoms that mimic psychiatric emergencies, such as panic attacks, psychosis, and catatonia, and that patients may be misdiagnosed and referred to mental health units instead of somatic units [N1-F1]. The same source notes that PE may also be masked by symptoms of mental disorders and that delayed diagnosis can be fatal [N1-F1]. In addition, the literature on non-cardiac chest pain notes that psychological conditions such as anxiety, panic disorder, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive disorder can manifest as chest pain, and that psychological distress can worsen physical pain [N5-R1][N5-R3]. This means that chest tightness in a psychiatric inpatient should be interpreted with caution: it can be genuine psychogenic chest pain, it can be a panic attack, or it can be a disguised organic condition such as PE [N5-R1][N1-F1].

### Bottom line for a senior nurse
In this case, chest tightness is most likely non-cardiac, especially anxiety or panic-related, but the psychiatric context raises the need for vigilance. The nurse should not dismiss it as purely “just anxiety,” because the same symptoms can also indicate PE, ACS, or other serious conditions [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The nurse should therefore screen for red flags and treat the patient as potentially unstable until the cause is clarified.

How to distinguish non-cardiac chest pain from cardiac or respiratory issues

Differentiating non-cardiac chest pain from cardiac or respiratory issues requires a focused comparison of symptoms and a structured workup, with ECG, oxygen saturation, and respiratory assessment often taking priority depending on the patient’s presentation.

### Symptoms that help differentiate panic attack from heart attack or asthma
The evidence shows that panic attacks and heart attacks share symptoms such as chest pain, rapid heartbeat, and shortness of breath, but their causes are different [N3-R2]. The asthma versus panic comparison is especially useful here: asthma and panic can both cause shortness of breath, chest tightness, feelings of intense fear, wheezing, chest pain, and sweating [N3-F3]. However, asthma is often associated with coughing, wheezing, mucus production, and symptoms that often improve with rescue inhalers [N3-F3]. Panic attacks are more likely to include shaking, trembling, dizziness, feelings of unreality, fear of losing control or dying, and symptoms that are often not relieved by bronchodilators [N3-F3]. The panic-disorder article also states that 22% to just over 70% of panic attacks are associated with chest pain [N3-R3].

For heart attacks, the warning signs include chest discomfort, arm, neck, and jaw pain, shortness of breath, and more [N1-R5]. The PE article adds that chest pain can be pleuritic, worsen with inspiration, cough, or trunk movement, or, less commonly, crushing, burning, or squeezing retrosternal pain [N1-F1]. In other words, if the chest pain is associated with sweating, dizziness, radiating pain, or a history of coronary disease, cardiac disease becomes more likely [N1-R5][N1-F1].

### When to prioritize ECG, oxygen saturation, and respiratory assessment
ECG should be prioritized if there is concern for ACS or any serious cardiac condition. The NICE guidance states that obtaining a focused medical history after assessing vital signs and ECG is appropriate, and that chest pain should be managed with a 12-lead ECG when ACS is suspected [N2-R1]. Oxygen saturation should be checked because low oxygen saturation can indicate respiratory compromise or PE [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The CKS guidance also emphasizes measuring oxygen saturation and using pulse oximetry as part of the physiological assessment [N2-F2]. Respiratory assessment should be prioritized if there are signs of asthma, COPD, or other pulmonary causes, because asthma can present with wheezing, coughing, and chest tightness that may mimic panic [N3-F3][N3-R5].

### When psychiatric symptoms may mimic organic disease
Psychiatric symptoms can mimic organic disease very clearly. The PMC article on PE notes that PE can manifest with psychopathological symptoms that mimic psychiatric emergencies, such as panic attacks, symptoms of psychosis, and catatonia, and that this can lead to misdiagnosis and delayed treatment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that PE may be masked by symptoms of mental disorders and that patients may be referred to mental health units instead of somatic units, delaying management and risking death [N1-F1]. The literature on non-cardiac chest pain adds that psychological conditions such as anxiety, panic disorder, phobias, and obsessive-compulsive disorder can manifest as chest pain, and that psychological distress can worsen physical pain [N5-R1][N5-R3]. This means that a psychiatric inpatient’s chest tightness may be a genuine psychogenic presentation, a panic attack, or a disguised organic condition.

### Bottom line for a senior nurse
To distinguish non-cardiac chest pain from cardiac or respiratory issues, ask: is the symptom more consistent with panic, asthma, or anxiety? Is there evidence of cardiac disease, PE, or respiratory compromise? If chest tightness is the main complaint, check ECG, oxygen saturation, and respiratory status early. Do not assume that psychiatric symptoms mean the patient is safe; they can mask serious disease and require careful screening [N3-R2][N3-F3][N1-F1][N2-R1].

Practical nursing steps to take next

As a senior nurse, the immediate next steps are to stabilize the patient, collect baseline information, and escalate care if needed. The evidence supports a structured approach that balances observation with timely intervention.

### What to do immediately before or while vitals are obtained
Before obtaining vitals, the nurse should sit the patient in a comfortable position and reassess the patient’s mental state and level of distress [N2-F2]. If the patient is visibly anxious or in acute distress, the nurse should provide reassurance and support while preparing for vitals. The nurse should also observe for signs of acute decompensation, such as altered mental status, severe respiratory distress, or chest pain that is worsening or radiating [N2-F2][N1-F1]. During vitals collection, the nurse should use the full set of vital signs: blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation [N4-R2]. The CKS guidance also emphasizes that these assessments should be repeated as needed and that early warning scores can help determine the timing of next observations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### When to call the physician or initiate emergency protocol
The nurse should call the physician or initiate emergency protocol immediately if any of the high-risk vital-sign findings are present: respiratory rate over 30, tachycardia over 130, systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg or diastolic less than 60 mmHg, oxygen saturation less than 92%, central cyanosis, altered level of consciousness, or raised temperature above 38.5°C [N2-F2]. The CKS guidance also says that suspected ACS, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, aortic dissection, and ruptured oesophagus require immediate admission because of high risk of death or serious morbidity [N2-F2]. If the patient is in the psychiatric ward, the nurse should also consider PE as a red flag because psychiatric patients are at higher risk of delayed diagnosis and misdiagnosis [N1-F1]. In addition, if the patient has new symptoms such as sweating, dizziness, or chest pain that radiates to the arm, the nurse should treat the situation as an emergency [N1-R5].

### How to communicate with the patient and family if needed
Communication should be calm, clear, and reassuring. The nurse should explain that chest tightness can have many causes, including anxiety or heart-related issues, and that checking vitals is important to determine whether further action is needed [N2-R1]. The nurse should also inform the patient that the healthcare team is assessing them carefully and that they will be treated as needed to ensure safety [N2-R1]. If family members are present, the nurse should involve them in the explanation while preserving patient privacy and avoiding unnecessary alarm. In the psychiatric setting, communication should also acknowledge the patient’s mental state and any history of anxiety or panic, because those factors may influence the presentation and interpretation of symptoms [N5-R3][N3-F3]. The nurse should document the conversation, including any reassurance provided and any family involvement, to ensure continuity of care.

### Bottom line for a senior nurse
The immediate nursing steps are: sit the patient comfortably, reassess distress and mental status, obtain baseline vitals, and call the physician or initiate emergency protocol if any high-risk signs are present. If the patient is stable, continue observation, repeat vital signs, and communicate clearly with the patient and family while remaining alert for deterioration [N2-F2][N4-R2][N2-R1].
